notes.front: What is istioctl?
notes.back: Istio’s command-line tool for installing and customising the Istio control plane and the sidecars of the data plane.
notes.explanation: It validates user input to help prevent installation errors and lets you override any aspect of the configuration.
notes.example: Like kubectl, but aimed at installing and operating Istio itself rather than general cluster objects.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Install with Istioctl”, introduction
notes.evidence: This installation guide uses the istioctl command line tool to provide rich customization of the Istio control plane and of the sidecars for the Istio data plane. It has user input validation to help prevent installation errors and customization options to override any aspect of the configuration.

notes.front: What is an Istio configuration profile?
notes.back: A named group of Helm chart value overrides, built into the charts, usable when installing with either Helm or istioctl.
notes.explanation: Profiles give high-level customisation of the control plane and data plane for common deployment topologies and target platforms.
notes.example: Like choosing “economy” or “sport” mode on a car: one name sets many dials at once, and you can still adjust any dial afterwards.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Installation Configuration Profiles”, introduction
notes.evidence: Configuration profiles are simply named groups of Helm chart value overrides that are built into the charts, and can be used when installing via either helm or istioctl. The profiles provide high-level customization of the Istio control plane and data plane for common deployment topologies and target platforms.

notes.front: What is the IstioOperator API?
notes.back: The complete API that istioctl install provides for customising an Istio installation, set with --set options or a file passed with -f.
notes.explanation: It is the full user configuration of an install, written as an IstioOperator custom resource.
notes.example: Like a single order form for the whole install: tick options one by one on the command line, or hand in the completed form as a file.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Customizing the installation configuration”, introduction
notes.evidence: In addition to installing any of Istio’s built-in configuration profiles, istioctl install provides a complete API for customizing the configuration. The IstioOperator API The configuration parameters in this API can be set individually using --set options on the command line.

notes.front: What is sidecar injection in Istio?
notes.back: Adding the Istio sidecar proxy to a pod, either automatically in the pod’s namespace or manually with istioctl.
notes.explanation: Pods in the mesh must run an Istio sidecar proxy to take advantage of all of Istio’s features in sidecar mode.
notes.example: Like a hotel adding a concierge to every room as it is booked, instead of guests arranging their own.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Installing the Sidecar”, section “Injection”
notes.evidence: In order to take advantage of all of Istio’s features, pods in the mesh must be running an Istio sidecar proxy. The following sections describe two ways of injecting the Istio sidecar into a pod: enabling automatic Istio sidecar injection in the pod’s namespace, or by manually using the istioctl command.

notes.front: What is the Istio CNI node agent?
notes.back: The component, installed by the cni chart, that detects pods belonging to the ambient mesh and configures traffic redirection between them and ztunnel.
notes.explanation: In an ambient Helm install it is part of the control plane step, installed before the ztunnel DaemonSet.
notes.example: Like a points operator on a railway: it does not carry passengers, but sets the switches so trains reach the right track.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Ambient mode: Install with Helm”, section “CNI node agent”
notes.evidence: The cni chart installs the Istio CNI node agent. It is responsible for detecting the pods that belong to the ambient mesh, and configuring the traffic redirection between pods and the ztunnel node proxy (which will be installed later).

notes.front: What is an Istio revision?
notes.back: An installation setting that lets several independent control planes run at once; each revision is a full control plane with its own Deployment and Service.
notes.explanation: Installing a new version under a different revision, next to the old one, is how a canary control plane is started.
notes.example: Like two editions of a textbook on the same shelf: readers can be moved from the old edition to the new one class by class.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Canary Upgrades”, introduction
notes.evidence: the revision installation setting can be used to deploy multiple independent control planes at the same time. A canary version of an upgrade can be started by installing the new Istio version’s control plane next to the old one, using a different revision setting. Each revision is a full Istio control plane implementation with its own Deployment, Service, etc.

notes.front: What is a canary upgrade of Istio?
notes.back: Running the new control plane alongside the old one, moving a small share of workloads to it first, then migrating the rest.
notes.explanation: It lets you watch the upgrade’s effect on a small share of workloads; Istio calls it much safer than in-place and recommends it.
notes.example: Like opening a new bridge to a few lanes of traffic before closing the old bridge.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Canary Upgrades”, introduction
notes.evidence: Upgrading Istio can be done by first running a canary deployment of the new control plane, allowing you to monitor the effect of the upgrade with a small percentage of the workloads before migrating all of the traffic to the new version. This is much safer than doing an in-place upgrade and is the recommended upgrade method.

notes.front: What is a revision tag (stable revision label)?
notes.back: A stable identifier that points to a revision, so namespaces labelled with the tag move when the tag is pointed at a new revision.
notes.explanation: It exists because manually relabelling namespaces when moving them to a new revision can be tedious and error-prone.
notes.example: Like a “current-release” shortcut on a desktop: users click the same shortcut while you change which folder it opens.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Canary Upgrades”, section “Stable revision labels”
notes.evidence: Manually relabeling namespaces when moving them to a new revision can be tedious and error-prone. Revision tags solve this problem. Revision tags are stable identifiers that point to revisions and can be used to avoid relabeling namespaces.

notes.front: What is an in-place upgrade of Istio?
notes.back: Upgrading the existing control plane directly with the istioctl upgrade command, which can also downgrade.
notes.explanation: The same page notes that a canary upgrade is safer and is the recommended method.
notes.example: Like replacing an engine part while the car stays on the road, rather than driving a second car alongside first.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “In-place Upgrades”, introduction
notes.evidence: The istioctl upgrade command performs an upgrade of Istio. Canary Upgrade is safer than doing an in-place upgrade and is the recommended upgrade method. The upgrade command can also perform a downgrade of Istio.

notes.front: What does running istioctl install with no options install, and where?
notes.back: The default configuration profile, on the cluster defined by your Kubernetes configuration.
notes.explanation: The default profile is a good starting point for production, unlike the larger demo profile meant for evaluating features.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Install with Istioctl”, section “Install Istio using the default profile”
notes.evidence: This command installs the default profile on the cluster defined by your Kubernetes configuration. The default profile is a good starting point for establishing a production environment, unlike the larger demo profile that is intended for evaluating a broad set of Istio features.

notes.front: You are writing the production install for Istio with istioctl and have several settings to change. Which approach does the documentation strongly recommend?
notes.back: B: put the settings in a configuration file and pass it with -f.
notes.explanation: The page says --set and -f are equivalent, and uses --set in examples only to keep them compact; -f is strongly recommended for production.
notes.choices:
A) A long chain of --set flags on the command line
B) A configuration file passed with -f
C) Editing the compiled-in charts
notes.choicesExplained: A is equivalent in effect but is not the recommended production approach. C is unnecessary: compiled-in charts are the recommended default and settings are passed on top of them.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Install with Istioctl”, section “Install Istio using the default profile”
notes.evidence: The two methods are equivalent, but -f is strongly recommended for production.

notes.front: To install the demo profile with istioctl, run: istioctl install {{c1::--set profile=demo}}
notes.back: --set profile=demo
notes.explanation: Other configuration profiles are installed by passing the profile name on the command line in this way.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Install with Istioctl”, section “Install a different profile”
notes.evidence: Other Istio configuration profiles can be installed in a cluster by passing the profile name on the command line. For example, the following command can be used to install the demo profile: $ istioctl install --set profile=demo

notes.front: You install the default profile but need one of its values changed. What does Istio’s documentation say you can do?
notes.back: C: override that value with a --set flag placed after the profile in the command.
notes.explanation: Profiles compose with other value overrides and flags, so any single value a profile sets can be overridden.
notes.choices:
A) Switch to the empty profile and rebuild everything
B) Create a new named profile first
C) Override it with a --set flag after the profile
notes.choicesExplained: B is possible but not needed: the page states a --set flag overrides any individual profile value. C throws away the profile instead of overriding one value.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Installation Configuration Profiles”, introduction
notes.evidence: Configuration profiles compose with other values overrides or flags, so any individual value a configuration profile sets can be manually overridden by specifying a --set flag after it in the command.

notes.front: What does istioctl manifest generate produce, and what is it useful for?
notes.back: The install manifest, without installing it; useful to inspect exactly what is installed and to track changes over time.
notes.explanation: Unlike the IstioOperator resource alone, its output also captures changes in the underlying charts.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Install with Istioctl”, section “Generate a manifest before installation”
notes.evidence: The generated manifest can be used to inspect what exactly is installed as well as to track changes to the manifest over time. While the IstioOperator CR represents the full user configuration and is sufficient for tracking it, the output from manifest generate also captures possible changes in the underlying charts

notes.front: If you manage Istio by applying istioctl manifest generate output with kubectl, what must you do yourself that istioctl install does automatically?
notes.back: Remove resources that should go when the configuration changes; istioctl install prunes them automatically.
notes.explanation: Other caveats: create the Istio namespace manually, and Istio validation is not enabled by default.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Install with Istioctl”, section “Generate a manifest before installation”
notes.evidence: istioctl install automatically prunes any resources that should be removed when the configuration changes (e.g. if you remove a gateway). This does not happen when you use istio manifest generate with kubectl and these resources must be removed manually.

notes.front: What does the --purge flag add to istioctl uninstall, and is the istio-system namespace removed?
notes.back: --purge removes all Istio resources, including cluster-scoped ones that may be shared with other control planes. The namespace is not removed by default.
notes.explanation: Without --purge, you pass your original installation options to remove only that specific control plane.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Install with Istioctl”, section “Uninstall Istio”
notes.evidence: The optional --purge flag will remove all Istio resources, including cluster-scoped resources that may be shared with other Istio control planes. Alternatively, to remove only a specific Istio control plane, run the following command: $ istioctl uninstall <your original installation options>

notes.front: In a Helm install of Istio, what does the base chart contain, and when must it be installed?
notes.back: The cluster-wide custom resource definitions; it must be installed before the Istio control plane is deployed.
notes.explanation: The general pattern is helm install <release> <chart> --namespace <namespace>, starting with istio/base.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Install with Helm”, section “Installation steps”
notes.evidence: Install the Istio base chart which contains cluster-wide Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) which must be installed prior to the deployment of the Istio control plane

notes.front: Which Istio Helm chart deploys the istiod service?
notes.back: The Istio discovery chart, istio/istiod (for example: helm install istiod istio/istiod -n istio-system --wait).
notes.explanation: It follows the base chart; if you use the Istio CNI chart, that must be installed before istiod.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Install with Helm”, section “Installation steps”
notes.evidence: If you intend to use Istio CNI chart you must do so now. See Install Istio with the CNI plugin for more info. Install the Istio discovery chart which deploys the istiod service: $ helm install istiod istio/istiod -n istio-system --wait

notes.front: Which Istio Helm chart differs from the one istioctl uses?
notes.back: The gateway chart (istio/gateway). The other Helm charts are the same ones istioctl uses.
notes.explanation: The gateway chart is installed last, into its own namespace, after base and istiod.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Install with Helm”, introduction
notes.evidence: The Helm charts used in this guide are the same as those used when installing Istio via Istioctl, with the exception of the gateway chart. Istioctl uses a different gateway chart than the gateway chart described in this guide

notes.front: You are installing sidecar-mode Istio with Helm on a new cluster. Which chart goes first?
notes.back: B: istio/base, because it holds the cluster-wide custom resource definitions needed before the control plane.
notes.explanation: The guide installs base, then istiod, then (optionally) the gateway chart.
notes.choices:
A) istio/istiod
B) istio/base
C) istio/gateway
notes.choicesExplained: A is second: istiod needs the definitions from base to exist first. B comes last, after the control plane is running.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Install with Helm”, section “Installation steps”
notes.evidence: Install the Istio base chart which contains cluster-wide Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) which must be installed prior to the deployment of the Istio control plane

notes.front: When installing the Istio base chart for a revisioned installation, which value must be set, and why?
notes.back: --set defaultRevision=<revision>, so that resource validation works.
notes.explanation: The guide’s example installs the default revision, so it sets defaultRevision=default.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Install with Helm”, section “Installation steps”
notes.evidence: When performing a revisioned installation, the base chart requires the --set defaultRevision=<revision> value to be set for resource validation to function.

notes.front: Which label must the namespace of a Helm-installed Istio gateway not carry?
notes.back: istio-injection=disabled.
notes.explanation: The guide points to its “Controlling the injection policy” section for more on that label.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Install with Helm”, section “Installation steps”
notes.evidence: The namespace the gateway is deployed in must not have a istio-injection=disabled label.

notes.front: How can Helm adopt an Istio installation made with istioctl without uninstalling it?
notes.back: Install the charts with the --take-ownership flag, which adopts the existing resources in place.
notes.explanation: This avoids uninstalling and reinstalling Istio; backing up Istio resources first is highly recommended.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Install with Helm”, section “Migrating from non-Helm installations”
notes.evidence: If you’re migrating from a version of Istio installed using istioctl to Helm, you can have Helm adopt the existing resources in-place using the --take-ownership flag. This avoids the need to uninstall and reinstall Istio

notes.front: How do you find the configurable options of an Istio Helm chart, and apply changes after install?
notes.back: Run helm show values istio/<chart>; then apply overrides through the Helm upgrade workflow.
notes.explanation: Override settings can be given for any of the Istio Helm charts.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Install with Helm”, section “Updating your Istio configuration”
notes.evidence: You can provide override settings specific to any Istio Helm chart used above and follow the Helm upgrade workflow to customize your Istio mesh installation. The available configurable options can be found by using helm show values istio/<chart>

notes.front: While uninstalling a Helm-managed Istio, a colleague proposes deleting the Istio custom resource definitions too. What is the risk?
notes.back: B: Kubernetes cascade-deletes every resource of those types, such as your routing and authorisation resources.
notes.explanation: The Helm guide warns that deleting the Istio definitions permanently removes the Istio resources you created; deleting a chart with Helm leaves them in place by design.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, because Helm recreates them
B) All resources of those types are cascade-deleted
C) Only the istiod Deployment is affected
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: deleting the definitions permanently removes the Istio resources created from them. C is wrong: the loss covers every resource of those types, not one Deployment.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Install with Helm”, section “Migrating from non-Helm installations”
notes.evidence: When uninstalling, do not remove the Istio CRDs — deleting CRDs causes Kubernetes to cascade-delete all resources of those types

notes.front: What does an istioctl configuration profile do that the same profile used with Helm does not?
notes.back: It also selects which Istio components to install, so one istioctl command is enough; with Helm you install each component yourself.
notes.explanation: The profiles share names and values in both tools; only istioctl adds the component choice.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Installation Configuration Profiles”, introduction
notes.evidence: Note that a key difference between helm and istioctl install mechanisms is that istioctl configuration profiles also include a list of Istio components that will be installed automatically by istioctl. With helm, this is not the case - users are expected to install each required Istio component individually via helm install

notes.front: What are the two kinds of configuration profile, and what does each provide?
notes.back: Deployment profiles: good defaults for a deployment topology. Platform profiles: platform-specific defaults for a target platform. Using both is recommended.
notes.explanation: Examples given are default, remote and ambient for deployment profiles, and eks, gke and openshift for platform profiles.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Installation Configuration Profiles”, introduction
notes.evidence: There are 2 kinds of configuration profiles: deployment profiles and platform profiles, and using both is recommended. deployment profiles are intended to provide good defaults for a given deployment topology (default, remote, ambient, etc). platform profiles are intended to provide necessary platform-specific defaults, for a given target platform (eks, gke, openshift, etc).

notes.front: You install Istio with Helm on a managed Kubernetes platform, using a deployment profile and a platform profile. Where do you set them?
notes.back: A: on every chart you install, supplying the same profile and platform each time.
notes.explanation: With Helm, each component is installed separately, so each one needs the profile flags.
notes.choices:
A) On every chart, with the same values
B) Only on the base chart
C) Only on the istiod chart
notes.choicesExplained: B and C leave the other charts without the profile values: Helm does not choose or configure components for you, unlike istioctl.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Installation Configuration Profiles”, introduction
notes.evidence: For Helm, supply the same profile and platform for every chart you install

notes.front: Which deployment profile is recommended for production deployments?
notes.back: default: it enables components according to the default settings of the IstioOperator API.
notes.explanation: It is also the profile recommended for primary clusters in a multicluster mesh.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Installation Configuration Profiles”, section “Deployment Profiles”
notes.evidence: default: enables components according to the default settings of the IstioOperator API. This profile is recommended for production deployments

notes.front: Which deployment profile showcases Istio with modest resource requirements but is unsuitable for performance tests?
notes.back: demo, which enables high levels of tracing and access logging.
notes.explanation: It is the profile installed by the quick start instructions and can run the Bookinfo application.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Installation Configuration Profiles”, section “Deployment Profiles”
notes.evidence: demo: configuration designed to showcase Istio functionality with modest resource requirements. It is suitable to run the Bookinfo application and associated tasks. This is the configuration that is installed with the quick start instructions. This profile enables high levels of tracing and access logging so it is not suitable for performance tests.

notes.front: Which deployment profile is the same as default but installs only the control plane components?
notes.back: minimal.
notes.explanation: This lets you configure the control plane and data plane components, such as gateways, with separate profiles.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Installation Configuration Profiles”, section “Deployment Profiles”
notes.evidence: minimal: same as the default profile, but only the control plane components are installed. This allows you to configure the control plane and data plane components (e.g., gateways) using separate profiles.

notes.front: Which deployment profile configures a cluster that connects to a control plane outside that cluster?
notes.back: remote.
notes.explanation: The control plane may run in a primary cluster or be an external control plane.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Installation Configuration Profiles”, section “Deployment Profiles”
notes.evidence: remote: used for configuring a cluster that connects to a control plane residing outside of the cluster.

notes.front: Which deployment profile is designed to help you get started with ambient mode?
notes.back: ambient.
notes.explanation: The ambient install guide uses it with istioctl install --set profile=ambient.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Installation Configuration Profiles”, section “Deployment Profiles”
notes.evidence: ambient: the ambient profile is designed to help you get started with ambient mode.

notes.front: Which deployment profile deploys nothing, and what is it useful for?
notes.back: empty; it can serve as a base profile for custom configuration.
notes.explanation: It is one of seven built-in deployment profiles, alongside default, demo, minimal, remote, preview and ambient.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Installation Configuration Profiles”, section “Deployment Profiles”
notes.evidence: empty: deploys nothing. This can be useful as a base profile for custom configuration.

notes.front: Which deployment profile contains experimental features, with stability, security and performance not guaranteed?
notes.back: preview.
notes.explanation: It is intended for exploring new features coming to Istio, at your own risk.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Installation Configuration Profiles”, section “Deployment Profiles”
notes.evidence: preview: the preview profile contains features that are experimental. This is intended to explore new features coming to Istio. Stability, security, and performance are not guaranteed - use at your own risk.

notes.front: A team will run load tests to measure mesh latency and wants a production-like install. Which profile should they avoid?
notes.back: B: demo, because its high levels of tracing and access logging make it unsuitable for performance tests.
notes.explanation: The default profile is the one recommended for production deployments.
notes.choices:
A) default
B) demo
C) minimal
notes.choicesExplained: B is the profile recommended for production. C is the default profile without data plane components, not one flagged as unsuitable for performance tests.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Installation Configuration Profiles”, section “Deployment Profiles”
notes.evidence: This profile enables high levels of tracing and access logging so it is not suitable for performance tests. minimal: same as the default profile, but only the control plane components are installed.

notes.front: How do you apply the gke platform profile with istioctl, and how with Helm?
notes.back: istioctl: --set values.global.platform=gke. Helm: --set global.platform=gke on each chart.
notes.explanation: Platform profiles set chart options required or recommended for a given environment, such as gke, eks, openshift or minikube, among others.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Installation Configuration Profiles”, introduction
notes.evidence: For Helm, supply the same profile and platform for every chart you install, for example istiod: $ helm install istiod istio/istiod -n istio-system --set profile=default --set global.platform=gke --wait For istioctl, supply the same profile and platform as arguments: $ istioctl install --set profile=default --set values.global.platform=gke

notes.front: You want istioctl install to set a legacy Helm option, pilot.traceSampling, from the command line. How do you write the flag?
notes.back: C: --set values.pilot.traceSampling=<value>, prefixing the Helm option name with “values.”.
notes.explanation: Previous Helm installation options are still supported, except Kubernetes resource settings, provided the name starts with values.
notes.choices:
A) --set pilot.traceSampling=<value>
B) --helm pilot.traceSampling=<value>
C) --set values.pilot.traceSampling=<value>
notes.choicesExplained: A lacks the values. prefix the page requires for Helm options. B is not a flag the page describes.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Customizing the installation configuration”, section “The IstioOperator API”
notes.evidence: For backwards compatibility, the previous Helm installation options, with the exception of Kubernetes resource settings, are also fully supported. To set them on the command line, prepend the option name with “values.”.

notes.front: Using the IstioOperator API from the command line, how do you disable the pilot component?
notes.back: --set components.pilot.enabled=false
notes.explanation: Each component’s settings live under components.<component name>, and the same setting can be written in an IstioOperator resource.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Customizing the installation configuration”, section “Identify an Istio component”
notes.evidence: For example, to use the API to change (to false) the enabled setting for the pilot component, use --set components.pilot.enabled=false or set it in an IstioOperator resource

notes.front: Where a parameter exists in both the Helm API and the IstioOperator API, which does the Istio community recommend, and why?
notes.back: The IstioOperator API, because it is more consistent, is validated and follows the community graduation process.
notes.explanation: Such overlap covers Kubernetes resources, namespaces and enablement settings, among others.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Customizing the installation configuration”, section “Customize Istio settings using the Helm API”
notes.evidence: Some parameters will temporarily exist in both the Helm and IstioOperator APIs, including Kubernetes resources, namespaces and enablement settings. The Istio community recommends using the IstioOperator API as it is more consistent, is validated, and follows the community graduation process.

notes.front: Under which IstioOperator path do you change a component’s Kubernetes settings, and what are two settings it covers?
notes.back: components.<component name>.k8s. Any two, for example: resources, replica count, PodDisruptionBudget, node selector.
notes.explanation: Every component has a KubernetesResourceSpec, and the settings use the Kubernetes API definitions.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Customizing the installation configuration”, section “Customize Kubernetes settings”
notes.evidence: The IstioOperator API allows each component’s Kubernetes settings to be customized in a consistent way. Each component has a KubernetesResourceSpec, which allows the following settings to be changed. Use this list to identify the setting to customize: Resources Readiness probes Replica count HorizontalPodAutoscaler PodDisruptionBudget

notes.front: Istiod needs more memory requested in a production install made with istioctl. Where in the IstioOperator resource do you set it?
notes.back: A: under components.pilot.k8s.resources.
notes.explanation: Kubernetes resource settings go through the IstioOperator API’s k8s section, not through Helm values.
notes.choices:
A) Under components.pilot.k8s.resources
B) Under values.pilot.resources
C) In the demo profile
notes.choicesExplained: A uses the Helm pass-through, and the page excludes Kubernetes resource settings from the legacy Helm options. C is a profile choice, not a per-component setting.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Customizing the installation configuration”, section “The IstioOperator API”
notes.evidence: If you want to set Kubernetes resource settings, use the IstioOperator API as described in Customize Kubernetes settings.

notes.front: The IstioOperator API includes a pass-through interface to the Helm API using the {{c1::values}} field.
notes.back: values
notes.explanation: Global and pilot settings, for example, can be configured through the Helm API this way inside an IstioOperator file.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Customizing the installation configuration”, section “Customize Istio settings using the Helm API”
notes.evidence: The IstioOperator API includes a pass-through interface to the Helm API using the values field.

notes.front: How are gateways defined in the IstioOperator API, and what must you always specify when overlaying one?
notes.back: As a list type, since several can be defined. From Istio 1.7 onward, the gateway name must always be given.
notes.explanation: The default profile installs one ingress gateway, called istio-ingressgateway, which can be customised like any other component.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Customizing the installation configuration”, section “Configure gateways”
notes.evidence: In the IstioOperator API, gateways are defined as a list type. The default profile installs one ingress gateway, called istio-ingressgateway. You can inspect the default values for this gateway. The built-in gateways can be customized just like any other component. From 1.7 onward, the gateway name must always be specified when overlaying.

notes.front: You need Helm values that differ for each of two user gateways. What does the documentation recommend?
notes.back: C: a separate IstioOperator resource (with profile empty) to generate a manifest for the user gateways.
notes.explanation: Helm values under spec.values.gateways are shared by all gateways of that kind, so per-gateway values need their own resource.
notes.choices:
A) Two installs of the demo profile
B) Different spec.values.gateways entries in the main resource
C) A separate IstioOperator resource for the user gateways
notes.choicesExplained: B does not work: those Helm values are shared by all gateways of that kind. C installs whole profiles rather than customising two gateways.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Customizing the installation configuration”, section “Configure gateways”
notes.evidence: Note that Helm values (spec.values.gateways.istio-ingressgateway/egressgateway) are shared by all ingress/egress gateways. If these must be customized per gateway, it is recommended to use a separate IstioOperator CR to generate a manifest for the user gateways, separate from the main Istio installation

notes.front: What do IstioOperator k8s.overlays do, and in what order are patches applied?
notes.back: They add, modify or delete resources in the generated manifest before it is applied. Patches apply in order, each on the previous output.
notes.explanation: Paths in patches that do not yet exist in the output manifest are created.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Customizing the installation configuration”, section “Patching the output manifest”
notes.evidence: Note that the patches are applied in the given order. Each patch is applied over the output from the previous patch. Paths in patches that don’t exist in the output manifest will be created.

notes.front: With the injection webhook enabled, setting the label {{c1::istio-injection=enabled}} on a namespace adds a sidecar to every new pod created there.
notes.back: istio-injection=enabled
notes.explanation: Istio provides the mutating webhook admission controller that adds the sidecars.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Installing the Sidecar”, section “Automatic sidecar injection”
notes.evidence: When you set the istio-injection=enabled label on a namespace and the injection webhook is enabled, any new pods that are created in that namespace will automatically have a sidecar added to them.

notes.front: How does automatic sidecar injection differ from manual injection?
notes.back: Automatic: an admission controller injects the proxy at pod creation time. Manual: istioctl modifies the configuration, such as a Deployment, directly.
notes.explanation: If you are not sure which to use, the documentation recommends automatic injection.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Installing the Sidecar”, section “Injection”
notes.evidence: When enabled in a pod’s namespace, automatic injection injects the proxy configuration at pod creation time using an admission controller. Manual injection directly modifies configuration, like deployments, by adding the proxy configuration into it. If you are not sure which one to use, automatic injection is recommended.

notes.front: After automatic injection is enabled, a colleague runs kubectl get deployment and sees no sidecar in the spec. Where should they look?
notes.back: C: at the individual pods, for example with kubectl describe; automatic injection happens at the pod level.
notes.explanation: Unlike manual injection, automatic injection does not change the Deployment itself.
notes.choices:
A) Injection has failed, so reinstall Istio
B) In the istio-sidecar-injector ConfigMap
C) At the individual pods
notes.choicesExplained: A is premature: a Deployment spec is not expected to change. B holds the injection template, not the injected result.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Installing the Sidecar”, section “Automatic sidecar injection”
notes.evidence: Note that unlike manual injection, automatic injection occurs at the pod-level. You won’t see any change to the deployment itself. Instead, you’ll want to check individual pods (via kubectl describe) to see the injected proxy.

notes.front: A namespace carries both istio-injection and istio.io/rev labels. Which one wins?
notes.back: The istio-injection label takes precedence.
notes.explanation: With control plane revisions, the istio.io/rev label (for example istio.io/rev=canary) is used instead of istio-injection.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Installing the Sidecar”, section “Controlling the injection policy”
notes.evidence: If the istio-injection label and the istio.io/rev label are both present on the same namespace, the istio-injection label will take precedence.

notes.front: If a pod’s namespace has no injection label and the pod has none either, is the pod injected by default?
notes.back: Generally not: it is injected only if enableNamespacesByDefault is enabled, which it is not by default.
notes.explanation: The injector injects when any injection label is enabled, and skips the pod when either istio-injection or sidecar.istio.io/inject is disabled.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Installing the Sidecar”, section “Controlling the injection policy”
notes.evidence: If neither label is set, the pod is injected if .values.sidecarInjectorWebhook.enableNamespacesByDefault is enabled. This is not enabled by default, so generally this means the pod is not injected.

notes.front: To inject the sidecar manually into a Deployment, run {{c1::istioctl kube-inject}} -f <file> and pipe the output to kubectl apply -f -.
notes.back: istioctl kube-inject
notes.explanation: By default it uses the in-cluster configuration; local copies can be passed with flags such as --injectConfigFile.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Installing the Sidecar”, section “Manual sidecar injection”
notes.evidence: To manually inject a deployment, use istioctl kube-inject

notes.front: You label a namespace with istio-injection=enabled while its pods are already running. What happens to those pods?
notes.back: Nothing until they are recreated: injection happens at pod creation time.
notes.explanation: The documentation’s own check deletes the running pod so that a new one is created with the sidecar (2/2 containers ready).
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Installing the Sidecar”, section “Deploying an app”
notes.evidence: Injection occurs at pod creation time. Kill the running pod and verify a new pod is created with the injected sidecar.

notes.front: Which pod label turns sidecar injection off for a single pod, even in an injection-enabled namespace?
notes.back: sidecar.istio.io/inject="false".
notes.explanation: The injector skips a pod whenever either istio-injection or sidecar.istio.io/inject is disabled.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Installing the Sidecar”, section “Controlling the injection policy”
notes.evidence: If either label (istio-injection or sidecar.istio.io/inject) is disabled, the pod is not injected.

notes.front: How do you override the injection template’s settings for one pod, and what image value is recommended?
notes.back: Add an istio-proxy container to the pod spec; injection treats it as an override. Set its image to auto.
notes.explanation: With image auto, the sidecar injector selects the image to use automatically.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Installing the Sidecar”, section “Customizing injection”
notes.evidence: While you can set a specific image to override the default one, it is recommended to set the image to auto which will cause the sidecar injector to automatically select the image to use.

notes.front: To install Istio with ambient mode support using istioctl, run: istioctl install {{c1::--set profile=ambient}} --skip-confirmation
notes.back: --set profile=ambient
notes.explanation: Support for ambient mode is included in the ambient profile.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Ambient mode: Install with istioctl”, section “Install Istio using the ambient profile”
notes.evidence: Support for ambient mode is included in the ambient profile. Install Istio with the following command: $ istioctl install --set profile=ambient --skip-confirmation

notes.front: Why must you check for the Kubernetes Gateway API custom resource definitions before an ambient install?
notes.back: They do not come installed by default on most Kubernetes clusters, so they must be installed before the Gateway API is used.
notes.explanation: Waypoint proxies, for example, are deployed using Kubernetes Gateway API resources.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Ambient mode: Install with istioctl”, section “Install or upgrade the Kubernetes Gateway API CRDs”
notes.evidence: Note that the Kubernetes Gateway API CRDs do not come installed by default on most Kubernetes clusters, so make sure they are installed before using the Gateway API

notes.front: On a fresh cluster you install the ambient profile, then try to create a waypoint, but kubectl reports no gateways.gateway.networking.k8s.io resource type. What was missed?
notes.back: C: installing the Kubernetes Gateway API custom resource definitions.
notes.explanation: Most clusters do not ship them, and waypoints are deployed using Gateway API resources.
notes.choices:
A) The istio-injection=enabled label
B) The demo profile
C) The Gateway API custom resource definitions
notes.choicesExplained: B is a different profile and does not add the missing resource type. C enables sidecar injection, which is unrelated to ambient waypoints.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Ambient mode: Install with istioctl”, section “Install or upgrade the Kubernetes Gateway API CRDs”
notes.evidence: Note that the Kubernetes Gateway API CRDs do not come installed by default on most Kubernetes clusters

notes.front: What does Istio intend for the Kubernetes Gateway API?
notes.back: To make it the default API for traffic management in the future.
notes.explanation: If you use the Gateway API, you do not need to install and manage the gateway Helm chart for ingress.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Ambient mode: Install with Helm”, section “Ingress gateway (optional)”
notes.evidence: Istio supports the Kubernetes Gateway API and intends to make it the default API for traffic management in the future. If you use the Gateway API, you do not need to install and manage an ingress gateway Helm chart as described below.

notes.front: Why are the control plane and data plane packaged and installed separately for ambient mode with Helm?
notes.back: To allow controlled upgrades.
notes.explanation: The ambient data plane is itself split into ztunnel and waypoints, so upgrades involve separate steps for each.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Ambient mode: Install with Helm”, introduction
notes.evidence: To allow controlled upgrades, the control plane and data plane components are packaged and installed separately. (Because the ambient data plane is split across two components, the ztunnel and waypoints, upgrades involve separate steps for these components.)

notes.front: In an ambient Helm install, which chart holds the basic custom resource definitions and cluster roles, and when is it installed?
notes.back: The base chart, installed before any other Istio component.
notes.explanation: The istiod, cni and ztunnel charts follow it, in that order.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Ambient mode: Install with Helm”, section “Base components”
notes.evidence: The base chart contains the basic CRDs and cluster roles required to set up Istio. This should be installed prior to any other Istio component.

notes.front: In an ambient Helm install, which profile value is passed to the istiod chart?
notes.back: profile=ambient (helm install istiod istio/istiod --namespace istio-system --set profile=ambient --wait).
notes.explanation: The istiod chart installs a revision of istiod, the control plane component that configures the proxies.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Ambient mode: Install with Helm”, section “istiod control plane”
notes.evidence: The istiod chart installs a revision of Istiod. Istiod is the control plane component that manages and configures the proxies to route traffic within the mesh. $ helm install istiod istio/istiod --namespace istio-system --set profile=ambient --wait

notes.front: Which Helm chart installs the Istio CNI node agent in an ambient install?
notes.back: The cni chart (helm install istio-cni istio/cni -n istio-system --set profile=ambient --wait).
notes.explanation: It is installed as part of the control plane step, before the ztunnel chart.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Ambient mode: Install with Helm”, section “CNI node agent”
notes.evidence: The cni chart installs the Istio CNI node agent. It is responsible for detecting the pods that belong to the ambient mesh, and configuring the traffic redirection between pods and the ztunnel node proxy (which will be installed later).

notes.front: Which Helm chart installs ambient mode’s node proxy, and as what kind of workload?
notes.back: The ztunnel chart, which installs the ztunnel DaemonSet.
notes.explanation: It is the data plane step of the ambient Helm install, after base, istiod and cni.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Ambient mode: Install with Helm”, section “ztunnel DaemonSet”
notes.evidence: The ztunnel chart installs the ztunnel DaemonSet, which is the node proxy component of Istio’s ambient mode.

notes.front: In an ambient mesh, pods are not having their traffic redirected to ztunnel. Which component is responsible for setting up that redirection?
notes.back: A: the Istio CNI node agent.
notes.explanation: It detects which pods belong to the ambient mesh and configures the redirection between them and ztunnel.
notes.choices:
A) The Istio CNI node agent
B) istiod
C) A waypoint proxy
notes.choicesExplained: A configures the proxies but does not set up per-pod redirection. C adds Layer 7 processing and only receives traffic after ztunnel.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Ambient mode: Install with Helm”, section “CNI node agent”
notes.evidence: It is responsible for detecting the pods that belong to the ambient mesh, and configuring the traffic redirection between pods and the ztunnel node proxy

notes.front: You install Istio 1.26.2 as a revision named after its version. Which revision value is valid?
notes.back: B: 1-26-2, because “.” is not a valid revision name character.
notes.explanation: The documentation suggests naming production revisions after the Istio version, with the dots replaced.
notes.choicesExplained: A and B both contain the “.” character, which is not allowed in revision names.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Canary Upgrades”, section “Control plane”
notes.evidence: However, you must replace . characters in the revision name, for example, revision=1-31-1 for Istio 1.31.1, because . is not a valid revision name character.

notes.front: To install a new control plane revision called canary with istioctl, run: istioctl install {{c1::--set revision=canary}}
notes.back: --set revision=canary
notes.explanation: Afterwards two control plane deployments and services run side by side, with a sidecar injector configuration for each.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Canary Upgrades”, section “Control plane”
notes.evidence: To install a new revision called canary, you would set the revision field as follows:

notes.front: Which command is recommended before upgrading Istio, to check the upgrade suits your environment?
notes.back: istioctl x precheck
notes.explanation: Both the canary and the in-place upgrade guides recommend running it first.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Canary Upgrades”, section “Before you upgrade”
notes.evidence: Before upgrading Istio, it is recommended to run the istioctl x precheck command to make sure the upgrade is compatible with your environment.

notes.front: After you install a new revision, what happens to the existing sidecar proxies?
notes.back: Nothing: installing the new revision has no impact on them until they are pointed at the new control plane.
notes.explanation: Which control plane a sidecar uses is decided during sidecar injection, from the namespace label istio.io/rev.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Canary Upgrades”, section “Data plane”
notes.evidence: However, simply installing the new revision has no impact on the existing sidecar proxies. To upgrade these, you must configure them to point to the new istiod-canary control plane. This is controlled during sidecar injection based on the namespace label istio.io/rev.

notes.front: How do you move namespace test-ns from istio-injection=enabled to the canary revision?
notes.back: Remove istio-injection and add istio.io/rev=canary, then restart the pods to trigger re-injection.
notes.explanation: The istio-injection label must go because, for backward compatibility, it takes precedence over istio.io/rev.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Canary Upgrades”, section “Data plane”
notes.evidence: To upgrade the namespace test-ns, remove the istio-injection label, and add the istio.io/rev label to point to the canary revision. The istio-injection label must be removed because it takes precedence over the istio.io/rev label for backward compatibility.

notes.front: You relabelled a namespace with istio.io/rev=canary, but its pods still report the old control plane. What is missing?
notes.back: B: restarting the pods (for example, kubectl rollout restart deployment -n <namespace>) so they are re-injected.
notes.explanation: Once re-injected, the pods are configured to point to the canary control plane.
notes.choices:
A) Deleting the old control plane first
B) Restarting the pods
C) Setting the canary revision as the default tag
notes.choicesExplained: B would remove the old control plane before workloads have moved, which the guide does only after both planes are upgraded. C changes the default revision but does not re-inject running pods.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Canary Upgrades”, section “Data plane”
notes.evidence: After the namespace updates, you need to restart the pods to trigger re-injection.

notes.front: To move every namespace labelled with tag prod-stable to revision 1-31-1, run: istioctl tag set prod-stable --revision 1-31-1 {{c1::--overwrite}}
notes.back: --overwrite
notes.explanation: No namespace relabelling is needed; restarting the injected workloads makes them use the new control plane.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Canary Upgrades”, section “Stable revision labels: Usage”
notes.evidence: namespaces labeled istio.io/rev=prod-stable can be updated with one action by modifying the prod-stable revision tag to point to the newer 1-31-1 revision. $ istioctl tag set prod-stable --revision 1-31-1 --overwrite

notes.front: Twenty namespaces are labelled istio.io/rev=prod-stable. The new revision has proved stable. What is the least error-prone way to move them?
notes.back: B: point the prod-stable revision tag at the new revision, then restart the workloads.
notes.explanation: Relabelling many namespaces by hand is tedious and error-prone, which is the problem revision tags solve.
notes.choices:
A) Relabel each namespace with the new revision name
B) Point the prod-stable tag at the new revision
C) Run an in-place upgrade of the old revision
notes.choicesExplained: A works but is the tedious, error-prone manual relabelling that tags avoid. C abandons the canary method and does not move namespaces between revisions.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Canary Upgrades”, section “Stable revision labels”
notes.evidence: Rather than relabeling the namespace, a mesh operator can simply change the tag to point to a new revision. All namespaces labeled with that tag will be updated at the same time.

notes.front: Which selectors does the default revision inject sidecars for?
notes.back: The istio-injection=enabled namespace selector, the sidecar.istio.io/inject=true object selector and the istio.io/rev=default selectors.
notes.explanation: The default revision also validates Istio resources and performs singleton mesh responsibilities, among its functions.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Canary Upgrades”, section “Default tag”
notes.evidence: The default revision performs the following functions: Injects sidecars for the istio-injection=enabled namespace selector, the sidecar.istio.io/inject=true object selector, and the istio.io/rev=default selectors Validates Istio resources

notes.front: When using the default tag alongside an existing non-revisioned installation, what should you remove, and why?
notes.back: The old MutatingWebhookConfiguration (typically istio-sidecar-injector), so the older and newer control planes do not both attempt injection.
notes.explanation: A revision is made the default with istioctl tag set default --revision <revision>.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Canary Upgrades”, section “Default tag”
notes.evidence: When using the default tag alongside an existing non-revisioned Istio installation it is recommended to remove the old MutatingWebhookConfiguration (typically called istio-sidecar-injector) to avoid having both the older and newer control planes attempt injection.

notes.front: With revision-based upgrades, jumping across {{c1::two}} minor versions is supported, for example from 1.15 directly to 1.17.
notes.back: Two.
notes.explanation: In-place upgrades, by contrast, must go through each intermediate minor release.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Canary Upgrades”, section “Before you upgrade”
notes.evidence: When using revision-based upgrades jumping across two minor versions is supported (e.g. upgrading directly from version 1.15 to 1.17). This is in contrast to in-place upgrades where it is required to upgrade to each intermediate minor release.

notes.front: A cluster runs Istio 1.24 and must reach 1.26 without stopping at 1.25. Which upgrade method allows this?
notes.back: B: a canary (revision-based) upgrade.
notes.explanation: Revision-based upgrades may jump two minor versions; in-place upgrades need each intermediate minor release.
notes.choices:
A) An in-place upgrade with istioctl upgrade
B) A canary (revision-based) upgrade
C) An in-place Helm upgrade
notes.choicesExplained: A and C are in-place upgrades, which require stopping at each intermediate minor release (here 1.25).
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Canary Upgrades”, section “Before you upgrade”
notes.evidence: When using revision-based upgrades jumping across two minor versions is supported (e.g. upgrading directly from version 1.15 to 1.17). This is in contrast to in-place upgrades where it is required to upgrade to each intermediate minor release.

notes.front: After both planes are on the new revision, how do you remove the old control plane of revision 1-30-1?
notes.back: istioctl uninstall --revision 1-30-1 -y
notes.explanation: If the old control plane has no revision label, uninstall it with its original installation options instead.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Canary Upgrades”, section “Uninstall old control plane”
notes.evidence: After upgrading both the control plane and data plane, you can uninstall the old control plane. For example, the following command uninstalls a control plane of revision 1-30-1: $ istioctl uninstall --revision 1-30-1 -y If the old control plane does not have a revision label, uninstall it using its original installation options

notes.front: To roll back by uninstalling the canary revision, what must you do first?
notes.back: Reinstall the previous revision’s gateways manually, using the old istioctl version, and make sure they are running.
notes.explanation: The uninstall command does not automatically revert gateways that were upgraded in place.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Canary Upgrades”, section “Uninstall canary control plane”
notes.evidence: However, in this case you must first reinstall the gateway(s) for the previous revision manually, because the uninstall command will not automatically revert the previously in-place upgraded ones.

notes.front: Can istioctl upgrade upgrade an installation made with the --revision flag?
notes.back: No. istioctl upgrade is for in-place upgrades; upgrades of revisioned installations fail with an error.
notes.explanation: The in-place prerequisites also require that Istio was installed using istioctl.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “In-place Upgrades”, introduction
notes.evidence: istioctl upgrade is for in-place upgrade and not compatible with installations done with the --revision flag. Upgrades of such installations will fail with an error.

notes.front: What does the in-place upgrade guide recommend to minimise traffic disruption?
notes.back: Run at least two istiod replicas, and configure PodDisruptionBudgets with a minimum availability of 1.
notes.explanation: The upgrade commands should be run with the new version of istioctl, found in the bin/ subdirectory of the downloaded package.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “In-place Upgrades”, section “Upgrade steps”
notes.evidence: Traffic disruption may occur during the upgrade process. To minimize the disruption, ensure that at least two replicas of istiod are running. Also, ensure that PodDisruptionBudgets are configured with a minimum availability of 1.

notes.front: You installed Istio with istioctl install -f custom.yaml. How should you run the in-place upgrade?
notes.back: A: istioctl upgrade -f custom.yaml, with the same -f value.
notes.explanation: If you omit -f, Istio upgrades using the default profile; customisations made with --set are reverted unless the same flags are passed.
notes.choices:
A) istioctl upgrade -f custom.yaml
B) istioctl upgrade --set profile=demo
C) istioctl upgrade with no flags
notes.choicesExplained: A upgrades using the default profile, dropping your custom configuration. B switches to a different profile instead of keeping yours.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “In-place Upgrades”, section “Upgrade steps”
notes.evidence: If you installed Istio using the -f flag, for example istioctl install -f <IstioOperator-custom-resource-definition-file>, then you must provide the same -f flag value to the istioctl upgrade command.

notes.front: For an in-place upgrade, the installed Istio version must be no more than {{c1::one}} minor version less than the upgrade version.
notes.back: One.
notes.explanation: For example, 1.6.0 or higher is needed before upgrading to 1.7.x; the installation must also have been made with istioctl.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “In-place Upgrades”, section “Upgrade prerequisites”
notes.evidence: The installed Istio version is no more than one minor version less than the upgrade version. For example, 1.6.0 or higher is required before you start the upgrade process to 1.7.x. Your Istio installation was installed using istioctl.

notes.front: istioctl upgrade finished successfully, but the sidecars still run the old proxy version. What step was skipped?
notes.back: A: restarting the pods with Istio sidecars, for example with kubectl rollout restart deployment.
notes.explanation: istioctl upgrades the control plane and gateways; the data plane must be updated manually by restarting the sidecar pods.
notes.choices:
A) Restarting the pods with Istio sidecars
B) Running istioctl x precheck again
C) Relabelling namespaces with istio.io/rev
notes.choicesExplained: A only checks compatibility; it changes nothing. C is the canary-upgrade method and does not apply to an in-place upgrade.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “In-place Upgrades”, section “Upgrade steps”
notes.evidence: After istioctl completes the upgrade, you must manually update the Istio data plane by restarting any pods with Istio sidecars: $ kubectl rollout restart deployment

notes.front: How do you downgrade Istio from 1.7 to 1.6.5 with istioctl?
notes.back: Run istioctl upgrade using the istioctl binary of version 1.6.5, the version you are downgrading to.
notes.explanation: The steps are identical to an upgrade; the target must be no more than one minor version lower and installed with istioctl.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “In-place Upgrades”, section “Steps to downgrade to a lower Istio version”
notes.evidence: You can use istioctl upgrade to downgrade to a lower version of Istio. The steps are identical to the upgrade process described in the previous section, only using the istioctl binary corresponding to the lower version (e.g., 1.6.5).

notes.front: In a Helm canary upgrade, what do you do after upgrading the base chart?
notes.back: Install a canary istiod chart with the revision value set, for example helm install istiod-canary istio/istiod --set revision=canary -n istio-system.
notes.explanation: The base chart’s cluster-wide resources are shared by the primary and canary installations.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Upgrade with Helm”, section “Canary upgrade (recommended)”
notes.evidence: Note that when you install a canary version of the istiod service, the underlying cluster-wide resources from the base chart are shared across your primary and canary installations.

notes.front: How do you finish a Helm canary upgrade once workloads have moved to the canary?
notes.back: Delete the old istiod release, then upgrade the base chart with --set defaultRevision=canary.
notes.explanation: This makes the new canary revision the cluster-wide default.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Upgrade with Helm”, section “Canary upgrade (recommended)”
notes.evidence: Once you have verified and migrated your workloads to use the canary control plane, you can uninstall your old control plane: $ helm delete istiod -n istio-system Upgrade the Istio base chart again, this time making the new canary revision the cluster-wide default.

notes.front: In an in-place Helm upgrade, which charts are upgraded, and how do you keep custom configuration?
notes.back: Base, then istiod, then optionally any gateway charts, with helm upgrade; add your override values file or options to each command.
notes.explanation: Adding the values file or custom options preserves your custom configuration during Helm upgrades.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Upgrade with Helm”, section “In place upgrade”
notes.evidence: You can perform an in place upgrade of Istio in your cluster using the Helm upgrade workflow. Add your override values file or custom options to the commands below to preserve your custom configuration during Helm upgrades.

notes.front: How do a canary upgrade and an in-place upgrade differ in safety and in how far they can jump?
notes.back: Canary: safer, recommended, may jump two minor versions. In-place: must pass through each intermediate minor release.
notes.explanation: Canary runs a second revision beside the old one; in-place replaces the running control plane with istioctl upgrade.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Canary Upgrades”, section “Before you upgrade”
notes.evidence: When using revision-based upgrades jumping across two minor versions is supported (e.g. upgrading directly from version 1.15 to 1.17). This is in contrast to in-place upgrades where it is required to upgrade to each intermediate minor release.

notes.front: How does labelling a namespace with a revision differ from labelling it with a revision tag?
notes.back: A revision label ties the namespace to one control plane. A tag label follows the tag, which can be repointed without relabelling.
notes.explanation: All namespaces labelled with a tag are updated at the same time when the tag changes.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Canary Upgrades”, section “Stable revision labels”
notes.evidence: Rather than relabeling the namespace, a mesh operator can simply change the tag to point to a new revision. All namespaces labeled with that tag will be updated at the same time.
